findings.breaking_input: A mock recording with `__failure: {class: "transport", exit: 0}` plus a contract-invalid output, routed through a chain whose only fallback is same-family (mock), on an explicit `--driver mock` run. Or: a `max_wall_ms` term equal to the current elapsed.
findings.why: The loop runs while `a.verdict !== "ok" && !overBudget()`. For an exit-0 contract fault, `classifyAttempt` returns `model-invalid`, which `nextHop` treats as hoppable across families. But `attempt()` is also called for the `model-invalid` same-tier retry; `max_wall_ms` check in `termsCheck` uses `ctx.elapsedMs >= t.max_wall_ms` which is already true when the term equals elapsed, so a valid hop or retry is refused as budget even though there is a clear attempt that could succeed. Worse, the exit-0 path writes `failureClass` via `mock` and `classifyAttempt` for code 0 with `contractFault` uses `model-invalid` — but the `__failure.class` is ignored for the purpose of the retry decision, so a driver that answers invalid JSON but declares `transport` never gets the cross-family hop (it is classified model-invalid and only hops once). The concrete break: a `max_wall_ms` equal to elapsed refuses a hop with the positive control at 1, contradicting the test's own `runRemainingMs: MIN_HOP_MS` boundary. This is the same off-by-one at-elapsed boundary the module's own test pins for MIN_HOP_MS.
findings.fix: Use `ctx.elapsedMs > t.max_wall_ms` (strict) or allow a hop when elapsed equals the term, and make the retry/loop share the exact same `termsCheck` used by `nextHop` without a second copy. Also ensure `contractHopped` is set on the same path as the cross-family hop so a post-loop rung-1 retry cannot double-count.

findings.breaking_input: A router row: `driver: mock, fallback: [generic-api], max_attempts: 2, max_wall_ms: 1, max_cost: unmetered` with a mock recording `__failure: {class: "transport"}` and the run budget `min=2`.
findings.why: The `max_wall_ms` check at `nextHop` uses `ctx.elapsedMs >= t.max_wall_ms`. When elapsed equals the term, the hop is refused as `budget`, but the module's own test claims `nh(["generic-api"], [hop("transport")], ctx({ runRemainingMs: FC.MIN_HOP_MS })).hop === true` and the timeouts are computed from a `max_wall_ms - elapsedMs` whose result 0 becomes `Math.max(1, 0)=1`, allowed to run. So the at-elapsed case is inconsistently both a budget stop and a startable hop depending on which cap is tighter — a chain whose `max_wall_ms` equals the elapsed time refuses a hop the run genuinely has time for, failing a promise the term allowed.
findings.fix: Make the wall term a strict less-than (`elapsedMs < max_wall_ms`) for starting a hop, matching the test's boundary at `MIN_HOP_MS` in both code paths, and have `termsCheck` return the same decision on both the hop and the retry path.

findings.breaking_input: A mock recording root with `__failure: {class: "transport", exit: 1}` and a `max_wall_ms` term of exactly the elapsed time, routed as `driver: mock, fallback: [generic-api]` (cross-family) — run with `--budget min=2`.
findings.why: `classifyAttempt` for a driver exit 1 reads the sidecar declaration and returns `transport`. `nextHop` then checks `HOPPABLE`, picks the target, and calls `termsCheck`. `termsCheck` refuses when `ctx.elapsedMs >= t.max_wall_ms`. The receipt is then emitted as `reason: budget` even though the attempt was a transport that the chain could have tried — the chain's own term is the only obstacle, but the receipt and the exit code (1) claim a budget outcome for a failure that never spent anything. This is the same "at the term is both a stop and a start" inconsistency as L1/L2, and it is the exact deadline-pair the test suite pins for `runRemainingMs` but not for `max_wall_ms`.
findings.fix: Use a strict `elapsedMs > max_wall_ms` for the refuse, and compute the started hop's timeout as `Math.max(1, max_wall_ms - elapsedMs)` only when that leaves a positive floor, so the term behaves identically to the run-remaining cap on both byTerms and timeoutMs.

findings.breaking_input: A chain with `fallback: [generic-api, codex]` where `generic-api` is the same family as the first driver, a mock recording `__failure: {class: "model-invalid"}`, with `max_attempts: 3`.
findings.why: For a `model-invalid` failure, `nextHop` skips the same-family entry and selects the first different-family entry. With `fallback: [generic-api, codex]` and families mock→mock, generic-api→openai (from its pin), codex→openai, none is different, so `index` stays -1 and `nextHop` returns `{hop:false, noFamily:true}`. The loop then exits with `chainStop` unset, and the schema ladder's rung 1 runs `termsCheck`; that passes, so the same-driver retry runs. That is the intended F1 path — two attempts. But the loop condition is `a.verdict !== "ok"`, and for the retry that failed, `a.failureClass === "model-invalid"` again; the post-retry code emits a proposal via the schema ladder, yet `attempts` is taken from `attemptsMade` (3), not from the two actual attempts, and `hops` length is 3. A reader counting `hops` for the chain's max_attempts sees a third attempt that was never a driver invocation.
findings.fix: Increment `attemptsMade` only under `attempt()`, and have the schema ladder read `attempts` from `HOPS.length`, not from a counter that can be incremented by the retry path without a hop. Also make `contractHopped` reflect the actual hop source so a retry after a no-family hop is not mislabeled.

findings.why:
When the loop breaks because `nextHop` returns `byTerms: false` for a non-hoppable class, `chainStop` is set but `chainStop.byTerms` is false, so no budget emit happens. The run then falls to the policy block. For a `policy-refusal` that is correctly not hoppable, that is fine. But the same path is taken when `nextHop` returns `byTerms: false` because the class is `unknown` — and `unknown` is also not hoppable. The only difference between `policy-refusal` and `unknown` on this path is the receipt's `failure_class`, yet `unknown` never gets a loud "this chain stops here" line, and a reader relying on `chainStop` for why-there-was-no-hop gets `why: "a unknown failure never falls back"` that is not surfaced anywhere. The test only pins the receipt, not the message.

More importantly: a policy-refusal with `max_attempts: 1` still increments `attemptsMade` to 1 and records a hop, and the `nextHop` terms check is never consulted for the FIRST attempt — so a row with `max_attempts: 1` still spends one attempt, contradicting the "refuse before spend" claim for the first attempt itself. The row's own term cannot bind its first attempt.
findings.fix: Surface `chainStop.why` on every non-hop before the policy/schema surface, and apply `max_attempts` to the first attempt as well (a row with `max_attempts: 1` should refuse dispatch entirely, or the term should mean "attempts after the first").

findings.breaking_input: A driver writes a `failure_class` sidecar with a non-string value, e.g. `failure_class: 5`, or a JSON number `5`.
findings.why: `readDeclared` warns and returns `unknown` for a non-string — good. But `classifyAttempt` for `code !== 0` uses `readDeclared(o.declared)` where `declared` may be any JSON. The `declared` value comes from the cost sidecar in `invoke()`, which parses the file with `JSON.parse`; a sidecar `{"failure_class": 123}` sets `declared = 123`, and `readDeclared` returns `unknown` with warn — correct. However `classifyAttempt` for `code === 0` with `contractFault` returns `model-invalid` regardless, and the mock driver's `__failure.class` is passed through unvalidated, so a recording with `class: {nested: 1}` reaches `attempt()` and `HOPS.push({class: c.cls})` where `c.cls` is `unknown` for an exit 1 but for exit 0 is `null` even though the sidecar declared. The test `ok U: exit 0 with a clean answer has no class whatever the sidecar declares` pins the null, but the `contractFault` branch pins `model-invalid` "whatever the sidecar declares" — inconsistent handling of the same sidecar value between the two exit-0 outcomes.
findings.fix: Classify the sidecar declaration once in `classifyAttempt` and make the exit-0 branches both ignore it consistently, or both honor it; never have one branch say "model-invalid whatever the sidecar declares" and the other "no class whatever the sidecar declares" for the same exit code.

findings.breaking_input: A run that reaches no driver (e.g. `--budget inr=0` or a pre-dispatch policy denial) where `HOPS` is empty and `payload.outcome` is "fail".
findings.why: `function emitRun` computes `failureClass = payload.outcome === "ok" ? undefined : (rest.failure_class ?? (lastHop && lastHop.class) ?? classForReason(String(rest.reason ?? "")))`. When `rest.failure_class` is set explicitly (the budget/exit paths in this diff), it wins. But for a pre-dispatch budget where the caller passes `failure_class: "budget"`, the field is written. For a run that never reaches a drive and emits via `fail()` with no explicit class, `classForReason` produces the class. That is fine. The real issue is that `rest.failure_class` can be `null` from `classifyAttempt` for a failing exit-1 that declared no class, and `null ?? ...` treats null as absent, falling back to `classForReason("")` → `unknown` — which is correct for "no declaration". But a run that succeeded (outcome ok) with a driver exit 0 and a sidecar declaring `transport` records `hops[0].class === null` and `rest.failure_class` string-wins; the receipt carries `failure_class: undefined` but `hops` includes the `null` class, and a reader that treats `null` and `undefined` differently will see a class on a successful run when the spec says a successful run has no class.
findings.fix: Force `failureClass` to `undefined` whenever `payload.outcome === "ok"`, regardless of `rest.failure_class` or `lastHop.class`, so the receipt never shows a class on success and the hops' null entries are consistent with it.

findings.breaking_input: A driver calls `writeFailureClass` with a class containing whitespace, e.g. `" transport "` or `"Transport"`.
findings.why: `writeFailureClass` writes the class verbatim to the sidecar. arc-run reads it via `readDeclared`, which only warns for a value outside the set. A string with trailing whitespace "transport " is outside `KNOWN` and becomes `unknown`, with the warn. That is the intended "driver typo surfaces as unknown" behavior. But the failing-class path in `common.mjs`'s catch writes the class only if `e.arcFailureClass !== undefined`; if a driver sets `arcFailureClass = null` (the mock's `class: null` case), it writes nothing and arc-run reads `unknown` — correct. The asymmetry: `mock`'s `__failure.exit: 0` returns `{output, failureClass: __failure.class ?? undefined}` and if `class` is `null`, `failureClass` is `undefined`, so nothing is written — but the mock's own `__failure: {class: "transport", exit: 0}` path would write `transport`, and arc-run's `classifyAttempt` for exit 0 ignores the sidecar (`return {cls:null}` for a clean answer). So a mock recording can FALSELY declare a failure class on a success, and the module's own m5 mutant test expects the `exit0` scenario to record a `transport` class in the hop — meaning the "ignore" rule is only enforced for the receipt's `failure_class`, not for the `hops[].class`. The hops record lies about the run.
findings.fix: In `classifyAttempt`, for exit 0 never set `cls` from the sidecar; and in `mock`, when `exit: 0`, null out the class before returning so `HOPS` records `null`, not the driver's declaration.

findings.breaking_input: A recording key `__failure: {class: "transport", exit: 2}` where the recording ALSO carries `__cost: {inr: 0, source: "measured"}`.
findings.why: In mock's replay, `__failure` is detected first, and for `exit: 2` it throws `e` with `arcExit = 2`. The cost sidecar is never written in that branch — the `if (__cost)` block below never runs. So an exit-2 (budget-declined) failure loses its `writeCost`, and arc-run's `inrSpent` is not incremented; the receipt's `reason: budget` is correct, but `max_cost` accounting for the run is missing the spent amount, violating "max_cost measures spend". The mock fixture `exit2-declares.json` in the test has no `__cost`, so the suite never measures this.
findings.fix: For `exit: 2`, write the `__cost` before throwing, exactly as the exit-1 path should; and have the test's `exit2` recording carry a cost to pin the accounting.

findings.breaking_input: A `generic-api` row with `max_cost: unmetered` and `fallback: [mock]` where the mock answers invalid JSON.
findings.why: `chainTermFaults` faults a row whose chain holds `mock` (a metering driver) with `max_cost: unmetered`. But the live `engine/router.yaml` rows that hold no metering driver are all `unmetered`, and `commit-msg-draft`'s chain is `[codex, generic-api]` — neither metering, so `unmetered` loads. A future edit adding `mock` to that chain (as the fixture does) would fault. The `max_cost` check in `termsCheck` only runs when `isTerm(t.max_cost)`, so an `unmetered` chain skips the money check entirely — meaning the check-in `nextHop` and the load-time `chainTermFaults` disagree about whether `mock` in a chain is allowed under `unmetered`. The load refuses it, the runtime would silently skip the money check if it did load. That is a "validate at load, enforce differently at runtime" twin.
findings.fix: Have `termsCheck` also treat a metering driver in an `unmetered` chain as a load fault (or refuse the hop) rather than silently skipping, and align the two checks on the same `METERING_DRIVERS` table.

findings.breaking_input: A chain `fallback: [generic-api]`, first driver mock, mock recording `__failure: {class: "model-invalid"}`, `max_attempts: 2`, and the generic-api server answering valid JSON on the FIRST call.
findings.why: The loop runs once for the model-invalid; `nextHop` picks generic-api (different family) and `termsCheck` with `max_attempts: 2` sees `hops.length + 1 > 2` is false (1 hop recorded, 1 future attempt = 2), so it hops. The second attempt succeeds, `a.verdict === "ok"`, loop stops. Correct. But if the second attempt at generic-api ALSO fails with `model-invalid`, the loop iterates again; `nextHop` sees `contractHops = hops.slice(0,-1).filter(class === "model-invalid").length` = 1, so it refuses, `chainStop` set with `byTerms: false`. The schema ladder then runs rung 1 (same-driver retry) because `contractHopped` was set true only when `a.failureClass === "model-invalid"` inside the loop — but AFTER the loop, `a` is the failed generic-api, so `a.failureClass === "model-invalid"` and `contractHopped` is set. The retry block checks `if (!contractHopped)` and skips the retry. Good. But the schema ladder then emits a proposal with the FIRST generic-api's `retry` variable still equal to `a` (the second failed attempt) and `driver` the last driver — correct. The defect: when the cross-family hop itself fails with `model-invalid`, `contractHopped` is set AFTER the loop exits on the hop's result, so the post-loop check `if (a.failureClass === "model-invalid") contractHopped = true;` runs once more and the retry is skipped — but `attemptsMade` already includes the hop, and the spec says a contract fault costs at most 2 attempts, never 3. Here it is 2 attempts on mock + 1 on generic-api = 3 hops in `HOPS`, and the receipt says attempts 3 — a reader would see 3 attempts for a "one extra attempt" guarantee.
findings.fix: Count the cross-family hop itself against the two-attempt budget, and refuse a second cross-family hop before starting it, not after — or record `contractHopped` at hop start so the loop cannot take a third.

findings.breaking_input: A contract fault (`model-invalid`) where the cross-family hop does NOT exist (noFamily) and the same-tier retry also fails as `model-invalid`, with `max_attempts: 2`.
findings.why: The loop for model-invalid finds no different family, `chainStop` has `noFamily: true`, `byTerms: false`. The rung-1 retry then runs: `termsCheck` with `max_attempts: 2` and `hops` currently `[mock]`, `hops.length + 1 > 2` is false (1+1=2), so it runs the retry, making attempts = 2. The retry fails `model-invalid` again; the schema ladder emits the proposal with `attempts` from `attemptsMade` = 2 and `hops` length 2. Correct. But if the retry instead SUCCEEDS, `a.verdict "ok"` is checked and the run reports success with `hops` length 2 — yet a successful retry after a model-invalid first attempt should not be possible because a model-invalid means the OUTPUT failed the contract; the mock's `__failure` with exit 0 can fabricate this. The mock's `exit: 0` path returns output AND declares failure, so the `contractFault` classifier sees exit 0 + the failed schema, classifies `model-invalid`, and the same tier retry runs — burning a second attempt on a failure the driver itself says is an output problem. The class `model-invalid` should mean "another model family might answer it" and the SAME model should not be retried at all, yet rung 1 retries the same driver.
findings.fix: For `model-invalid`, never run the same-driver retry — only a cross-family hop is allowed; if no family differs, go straight to the proposal receipt.

findings.breaking_input: A chain where the first driver is unknown (not in `DRIVER_FAMILY`) and reports `model-invalid`; the fallback is `generic-api` with a known family.
findings.why: `familyOf` for the unknown first driver returns "unknown". In `nextHop`, for `model-invalid`, `from = ctx.familyOf(last.driver) = "unknown"`, and the `findIndex` requires `from !== "unknown"` — so no cross-family hop, even when a genuinely different family exists. That is fail-closed by design. But the receipt records `hops[0].class === "model-invalid"` and `noFamily: true` on stop — the reader is told "model-invalid never falls back for a missing family", which is accurate but indistinguishable from "a real same-family situation". The actual defect: `generic-api` with a model id that carries no vendor prefix (`bare-model`) is classified "unknown" too, so a generic-api→generic-api hop across two different endpoints of the same driver is refused as same-family even though they are different providers. The family table conflates driver identity with provider identity for `generic-api`.
findings.fix: For `generic-api`, require the resolved model id to name a family, and treat a bare model id as a load fault or as "different from another bare" — never as the same family by default.

findings.why: `invoke()` reads `cost` with `JSON.parse`, then if it holds `failure_class`, destructures it out and sets `cost = null` when nothing else remains. If `inr` is a string, `cost` stays an object with `inr: "not-a-number"`, and `attempt()` builds `hopCost` filtering on `Number.isFinite(r.cost[k])` — so it drops it. That is fine. But `Number.isFinite("")` is false, so a blank `inr` is dropped, and `cost` remains `{inr:""}`; `hopCost` becomes `{}` and is omitted. The run's `inrSpent` is not incremented, so a chain with a metering driver never sees the spend — the `max_cost` accounting is bypassed. The ADR-0069 b5 rule says absent is never estimated; here a present-but-blank value is treated as absent, which is the same blank-read-as-zero/NaN defect pattern. The test only checks `Number.isFinite`, not that a blank is refused loudly.
findings.fix: Refuse a `cost.json` with a non-finite present `inr` (warn and skip the run if it would violate a metered chain), or scrub the blank to absent with a warning, and pin the blank `inr` with a fixture.
